doc.title: Henry Johnson interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995

title: Phrasing as conversation, with Freddie Hubbard
summary: Woods's professor advised hinting at the scale; Johnson says Freddie Hubbard prefers phrasing like conversation and he thinks in breaths.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: You know one professor that I studied with, he basically he said, you know he said let’s say you’re getting ready to play over this dominant seven with a flat nine or a sharp nine. And you’re getting ready to play symmetric diminished half step whole step. He said, don’t play the whole scale two octaves. In other words he said we know you know the scale, he said, hint at it and then give the audience some place to enter the music. Let the thing breathe long enough for them to enter. Because if they’re listening, you know, you try to create this give and take. But like you said, in musics where the volume is too loud, the beat is always too insistent and force that you never imply but always state it, then sometimes the listener doesn’t have a chance to participate.

Well a lot of times too, if like when I’m out on the road with Freddie Hubbard, and I always bug him because I want to know everything. And Freddie told me this himself, if you notice the thing about Freddie, he has the command to go either way. But he prefers to phrase. Because phrasing is like talking to somebody. You know if you’re going to play on that dominant seven flat five, why play a scale? You know the scale that it goes with, so why play [scats]. That really doesn’t mean anything except that you know what notes go on that chord. But if you play [scats] and they you answer somebody, and you’re talking, you’re conversing with the rest of the band, somebody in the band is going to answer you. And it becomes a constant conversation all the time, and the listeners get a chance to come into the fold because they are also becoming a part of the conversation. So you know I sort of think in phrases because when you’re singing, you’re singing in phrases. You’ve got to take a breath sometime. So I just think breath. And if I think breath, I know that people relate, because they breathe too.
